title: Tech Edition
dek: Spyro is being ported with a hybrid of matching decompilation and static recompilation, agent reliability is being measured across an operational lifetime, and small tools are learning to observe agent work without scraping the screen.

lead_stories.headline: OpenPete does not wait for a perfect decompilation before making Spyro native
lead_stories.summary: OpenPete is a native PC port of the original Spyro the Dragon that combines matched C from the ongoing decompilation with statically recompiled MIPS code for everything not yet recovered. Version 0.1.4 shipped August 17; Windows builds are published and Linux already builds from source.
lead_stories.why_it_matters: It turns preservation into an incremental pipeline: verified source replaces translated binary function by function, so a usable port can exist years before a 100% matching decompilation.

reader.standfirst: OpenPete combines two preservation methods that are usually treated separately: exact source reconstruction where possible, and ahead-of-time binary translation everywhere else.
body: A matching decompilation rewrites a game in C until the original compiler produces the same machine bytes. That gives unusually strong evidence that a reconstructed function represents what shipped.

Matching an entire game can take years. OpenPete fills unfinished regions with PSXRecomp, which translates retail PlayStation MIPS instructions into C; matched functions can replace those translated blocks as reverse engineering progresses.
The runtime keeps the original simulation at roughly 29.913 Hz and interpolates extra visual frames, so higher display frame rates do not simply speed the game up.
reader.context: The project requires the user's own game data and does not distribute commercial assets.
key_points: Verified source and translated binary can coexist in one port.
A narrow game/runtime boundary lets source recovery progress independently from host-platform work.
Interpolation can improve display smoothness without changing simulation speed.
reader.limitations: Timing and determinism still differ in edge cases, Windows is the published target, Linux is source-buildable, and macOS is planned.
reader.what_to_try: Read OpenPete's 29.913 Hz timing explanation, then inspect PSXRecomp to see what is translated automatically versus supplied by the compatibility layer.

lead_stories.headline: AgingBench treats an AI agent like a system that can decay after deployment
lead_stories.summary: AgingBench evaluates agents over repeated sessions instead of only from a fresh start. It separates compression, interference, revision and maintenance failures and can report whether information was lost during writing, retrieval or use.
lead_stories.why_it_matters: A persistent agent can pass a day-one benchmark and still become less reliable as memory is compacted, stale facts accumulate, truth changes, or maintenance rewrites state.

reader.standfirst: The useful shift is from asking whether an agent is good to asking how it fails after 10, 50 or 200 sessions.
body: The benchmark repeatedly gives an agent tasks, lets its memory policy update state, and probes whether facts and derived state survive later sessions.

Compression aging means useful details disappear during summarization. Interference means relevant facts are buried among similar history. Revision means changed truth is not propagated correctly. Maintenance means lifecycle operations such as recompaction cause regression.
The repository supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenHands and Cursor adapters plus custom memory policies, and emits an AgingCard diagnostic schema.
reader.context: Published results use controlled scenarios and hundreds of runs; they support the framing but do not prove every deployed agent will degrade identically.
key_points: Reliability is longitudinal, not only a snapshot.
Memory-policy choice can matter as much as model choice.
The same wrong answer may need a different repair depending on which stage failed.
reader.limitations: Scenario realism and benchmark scoring remain simplifications of open-ended production work.
reader.what_to_try: Run one MAPS-style workflow through repeated compaction and correction cycles and score whether settled decisions survive.

lead_stories.headline: umux watches agent completion signals in the terminal byte stream instead of guessing from the screen
lead_stories.summary: umux 1.0.2 is a cross-platform terminal workspace manager with tabs, split panels, session restore and notifications. Its agent-aware feature listens for OSC terminal escape sequences emitted by tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Aider.
lead_stories.why_it_matters: It is a small example of observability at a cleaner boundary: consume an explicit machine-readable event instead of polling processes or scraping visible text.

reader.standfirst: The interesting mechanism is not the terminal layout. It is how the app learns that a long-running agent needs attention.
body: OSC sequences are control messages embedded in terminal output. Tools can emit them for notifications without printing human-facing text.
umux runs a stateful parser beside the PTY stream, recognizes OSC 9;9, OSC 99 and OSC 777, converts them to events, and passes ordinary output through unchanged.
That avoids timer-based process polling and brittle text heuristics such as scanning the terminal for 'done'.
reader.context: Version 1.0.2 shipped August 27 with Linux, macOS and Windows builds; Linux/Wayland is the reference environment.
key_points: Explicit completion events beat screen scraping.
Observation can be side-band without mutating the stream.
Old terminal protocols already contain useful automation hooks.
reader.limitations: Agent-status display is not perfect, Windows SSH support is planned, and builds are unsigned.
reader.what_to_try: Use the AppImage during one long Codex or Claude Code task and compare its notifications with a plain terminal.

lead_stories.headline: A tiny ESP32 can train its own vision model instead of sending images to a cloud
lead_stories.summary: A research prototype trains, deploys and runs a small convolutional neural network entirely on an ESP32-S3-class microcontroller with 8 MB PSRAM. The implementation is roughly 1,750 lines of C++ and uses no external ML framework.
lead_stories.why_it_matters: It makes the whole learning pipeline inspectable on hardware small enough to hold in one hand: capture data, calculate gradients, update weights and run inference locally.

reader.standfirst: TinyML usually means training elsewhere and only running the finished model on-device. This prototype deliberately keeps training on the microcontroller too.
body: The system captures 64×64 images, trains a two-layer convolutional network with Adam optimization and runs inference on the same ESP32-S3 device.
The reported three-class training run takes about nine minutes and inference runs at roughly 6.3 frames per second.
Its main value is inspectability: memory placement, gradient accumulation, resize tables and weight persistence are visible rather than hidden behind a large framework.
reader.context: This is a constrained learning problem, not a substitute for large modern vision models.
key_points: Small local training is possible when the model and task are constrained.
Readable implementations expose mechanisms cloud pipelines hide.
Local learning can matter when privacy, connectivity or inspectability dominate accuracy.
reader.limitations: The demonstrated task is small and broader accuracy claims should not be inferred.
reader.what_to_try: Read the weight-loading priority and PSRAM layout before the model code; the hardware constraints explain much of the architecture.

items.headline: PSXRecomp turns unfinished PlayStation decompilations into runnable host code
items.summary: PSXRecomp statically translates retail PlayStation MIPS instructions to C so projects can run code that has not yet been manually decompiled.
items.why_it_matters: It creates an incremental bridge between opaque binary and verified source instead of making a port wait for total decompilation.
items.why_i_might_care: This is the reusable mechanism underneath OpenPete's ability to ship early.

items.headline: Flux treats file-manager responsiveness as an architecture problem
items.summary: Flux uses Rust, GTK4/Relm4 and asynchronous I/O for directory loads, thumbnails, archive browsing, content search, remote GVFS paths and background file operations.
items.why_it_matters: The repo includes 350+ tests and parser fuzzing while keeping expensive filesystem work away from the UI thread.
items.why_i_might_care: It is a practical Linux utility worth watching if Nautilus or Thunar workflows feel limiting.
items.limitations: Version 0.1.0 is still young; project-authored startup timings are not independent benchmarks.

items.headline: AgingBench uses one diagnostic schema for lab tests and supported production traces
items.summary: Its AgingCard representation is designed to describe both controlled benchmark runs and post-hoc trace analysis.
items.potential_connection: A common evidence schema for pre-deployment tests and live incidents could make MAPS reliability work easier to compare over time.

items.headline: Interesting research: evaluate the lifespan of the harness, not only the model
items.summary: AgingBench separates model ability from memory compression, interference, revision and maintenance effects that accumulate during operation.
items.why_it_matters: A system can degrade while its underlying model weights never change.
items.potential_connection: Add longitudinal regression tests around compaction, handoffs, corrections and maintenance events.

items.headline: Useful now: prefer explicit completion events over inferred agent state
items.summary: umux demonstrates a low-cost observability pattern: consume OSC completion signals emitted by the tool and keep the terminal stream otherwise untouched.
items.potential_connection: MAPS runners should prefer explicit task-state events from workers where possible, falling back to inference only when no event boundary exists.

items.headline: OpenPete uses decompiled source and translated binary side by side
items.summary: Matched Spyro functions replace statically recompiled functions as reverse engineering progresses, while the port remains runnable throughout.
items.why_it_matters: It makes preservation progress incremental rather than all-or-nothing.

items.headline: The underlying Spyro decompilation is active but unfinished
items.summary: TheMobyCollective/spyro-1 continues matching retail functions; July commits updated matching progress and cleaned up recovered functions.
items.why_it_matters: OpenPete's hybrid strategy has value precisely because matching work remains incomplete.

items.headline: umux gives tmux-like project organization to people who do not want tmux
items.summary: Named workspaces contain terminal tabs and split panes, persist across restarts and can notify when supported coding agents finish.
items.why_it_matters: It solves the practical 'which of these terminals needs me?' problem with a GUI surface.

items.headline: Flux browses archives and remote mounts through the same navigation model
items.summary: Its path layer handles ordinary directories, archive virtual roots and GVFS-backed remote locations while asynchronous operations avoid freezing the interface.
items.why_it_matters: The architecture is more interesting than another file-manager skin: different storage backends are normalized behind one UI.

items.headline: Training a vision model locally changes what a microcontroller can be
items.summary: The ESP32-S3 prototype includes data collection, optimization, weight storage and inference instead of treating the board only as an inference endpoint.
items.why_it_matters: Small devices can adapt locally in privacy-sensitive or disconnected settings if the learning problem is constrained.

items.headline: Unearthed: a reusable RISC-V module once powered an e-paper conference badge
items.summary: Antmicro's open badge splits a SiFive FE310 RISC-V module from an e-paper baseboard and includes NFC EEPROM, USB-JTAG/UART and optional Bluetooth.
items.why_it_matters: It is a clean example of designing event hardware so the compute module can survive beyond the badge itself.

items.headline: How OpenPete mixes decompilation and recompilation without running two games
items.summary: Both routes ultimately produce host-callable code behind the same runtime boundary. A matched function is compiled from reconstructed source; an unmatched function is generated from retail MIPS instructions. Calls can cross that boundary, so translated blocks can be replaced gradually.
items.why_it_matters: It converts a years-long reverse-engineering project into a continuously improving executable.

items.headline: Agent aging may be more useful than another single-number benchmark
items.summary: The AgingBench framing separates distinct degradation mechanisms and asks where repair should target after many sessions.
items.limitations: Half-life-style metrics will be highly sensitive to scenario design and memory policy.

items.headline: A wearable ring exposes the verification problem in screenless agent interfaces
items.summary: A CHI 2026 Microsoft Research prototype used touch and haptics to delegate tasks without a screen. In an 11-person exploratory study, simple delegation felt useful but confidence fell for complex workflows without visual or audio verification.
items.why_it_matters: Removing interface friction also removes evidence; delegation and verification pull in opposite directions.
items.limitations: The study is small and exploratory rather than a general usability result.

items.headline: Someone powered a CHIP-8 computer from a Stirling heat engine
items.summary: A hobby build couples a tiny Stirling engine to a generator producing roughly 150 mW, then budgets that power across an ESP32-C3, 128×64 OLED and keypad. Wi-Fi/Bluetooth are disabled and clock speed drops to 10 MHz when idle; it still runs CHIP-8 games and includes an editor.
items.why_it_matters: When energy is the hard constraint, software architecture becomes power budgeting: lower clocks, fewer radios, tiny displays and simple virtual machines.

sections.title: You Probably Didn't Know You Were Interested In This

items.headline: Human-agent interfaces have a verification-bandwidth problem
items.summary: The wearable-ring study suggests the more invisible automation becomes, the harder it is for a user to know whether a complex task is being done correctly.
items.why_it_matters: This connects interface design to agent governance: a low-friction interface is only safe when it still communicates enough state for appropriate trust.

items.headline: Terminal control codes are a tiny event bus hiding in plain sight
items.summary: OSC sequences were designed for terminal control and notifications, but umux shows how they can become structured side-band events for agent orchestration without parsing human-facing output.
items.why_it_matters: Old protocols often contain cleaner automation hooks than a new scraping layer.

items.headline: Extreme power limits can make old virtual machines useful again
items.summary: CHIP-8 is primitive by modern standards, but its tiny instruction set is a natural fit when the computer is literally powered by a tabletop heat engine.
items.why_it_matters: Constraints can revive old abstractions for reasons unrelated to nostalgia.

items.headline: Longitudinal reliability cards
items.summary: AgingBench records how capability changes over sessions and separates compression, interference, revision and maintenance failures.
items.potential_connection: Create a small MAPS aging suite that repeats handoffs, compaction, corrections and maintenance, then reports which stage failed rather than only pass/fail.

items.headline: Explicit worker completion events
items.summary: umux relies on machine-readable OSC notifications instead of guessing completion from screen content.
items.potential_connection: Prefer explicit task-state signals from agents/tools and preserve them in coordination evidence; use inferred state only as a fallback.

items.headline: Verification bandwidth as an authority constraint
items.summary: The wearable-ring study shows that low-friction delegation becomes harder to trust as workflows get more complex and feedback disappears.
items.potential_connection: MAPS interfaces should scale visible evidence and confirmation requirements with consequence and ambiguity rather than optimizing solely for fewer interruptions.

rabbit_hole.headline: Follow one Spyro function from retail MIPS to matched C
rabbit_hole.summary: Start with OpenPete's architecture, then open TheMobyCollective/spyro-1 and PSXRecomp. The goal is to understand how an unmatched function can run today and later be replaced by byte-matching source without changing the whole port.
